opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to scale, and to what kind of scale actually matters.

If you look at how robot data is collected today, most of it is teleoperation. You have a person driving a robot through a task, maybe with a VR headset or a puppet arm, and every demonstration costs real time, real hardware, and real attention. Even the largest efforts out there are in the range of thousands of hours. That sounds like a lot until you compare it to what made language models and vision models work, which is essentially the entire internet's worth of text and images. Robotics just doesn't have that, and I don't think we're going to get there by paying people to teleoperate robots one demo at a time.

Meanwhile, humans are doing manipulation constantly. Every day billions of people are cooking, folding laundry, opening doors, organizing their desks, fixing things. That is an enormous, continuously generated stream of physical-interaction data, and right now almost all of it just disappears. So the question I keep coming back to is: how do we capture even a small fraction of that, without asking people to change what they're doing?

That's why the "incidental" part matters to me. The moment you design a data collection protocol specifically for robots, you introduce friction. People have to set up equipment, follow instructions, perform tasks in a certain way. That limits who participates, how long they participate, and how natural the behavior is. If instead the data comes as a byproduct of daily life, say from wearable cameras or smart glasses people already want to use for other reasons, then the cost per hour drops dramatically and the diversity goes way up. You get different homes, different objects, different cultures, different ways of doing the same task. That diversity is exactly what robots need to generalize beyond a lab setting.

There's also a quality argument that people sometimes overlook. Task-specific data tends to be very clean and very narrow. Real-life data is messy: people make mistakes, they recover, they improvise, they multitask. That messiness is actually valuable, because a robot deployed in the real world will face all of it too.

Now, I'm not claiming human data alone solves the problem. There's a real embodiment gap. A human hand is not a robot gripper, and human videos don't directly give you motor commands. A lot of our research is about bridging that gap: figuring out what transfers, like task structure, object affordances, intent, and the rough motion of the hands, and then using a smaller amount of robot data to ground it in the robot's own body. So the picture I have in mind is kind of a pyramid. At the base, massive amounts of passively captured human experience. Above that, more targeted human demonstrations. And at the top, a relatively small amount of robot-specific data to close the loop.

If we get that right, robot learning stops being bottlenecked by how many robots and operators you have, and starts scaling with how much people simply live their lives. To me that's the only path that plausibly gets us to the kind of data scale that general-purpose robots will need.

r001.rationale: The response describes people performing manipulation throughout daily life, but does not say these actions happen without conscious thought.

r002.rationale: It says robot-focused collection protocols make people set up equipment, follow instructions, and perform tasks in prescribed ways, which limits natural behavior; it contrasts this with data captured as a byproduct of daily life.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is scale and diversity, and the fact that we will never get either by collecting data one robot task at a time.

Think about what it costs to gather robot demonstrations. You need a physical robot, a teleoperation rig, a trained operator, a scene you set up and reset, and then you get maybe a few hundred episodes a day if everything goes well. The data is very clean and very on-distribution for the robot, which is great, but it is also extremely narrow. It covers the handful of objects you bought, the one lab or kitchen you set up, and the few behaviors you decided were worth demonstrating. When you then ask the policy to generalize to a new home with new clutter, it falls apart, because it has simply never seen anything like that.

Meanwhile, humans are producing an enormous amount of manipulation data every single day just by living. People cook, fold laundry, open drawers, fix things, pack boxes. A lot of that is already recorded, in egocentric video datasets, in how-to videos, in what people film on their phones without thinking about it. Nobody did it for a robot. That is exactly the point. Because nobody was optimizing for a benchmark, the data has the messiness of the real world baked in: different lighting, different objects, different ways of holding things, mistakes and recoveries. That long tail is what you actually need to cover, and you cannot engineer it into a lab collection protocol, no matter how careful you are.

The trade-off, of course, is that incidental human data is not directly usable. There is no action label, the embodiment is different, the camera is wherever it happened to be. So a lot of our work is about extracting the useful structure, things like hand and object trajectories, contact events, task decomposition, affordances, and then using that as a prior or a representation that a small amount of robot-specific data can ground into actual motor commands. I think of it as the human data teaching the model what a task looks like and how the world responds, and the robot data teaching it how to execute with its particular body.

There is also a deeper reason I care about this. If we insist that every bit of training signal has to be collected intentionally for robots, we are implicitly limiting the field to whoever can afford large collection operations. Incidental data is essentially free and keeps growing on its own. Learning to use it well seems like a much more sustainable path toward robots that work in anyone's home, not just the ones that look like our lab.

r001.rationale: The response lists everyday manipulation activities, but does not say that much of human physical intelligence consists of actions people perform without conscious thought. “Without thinking about it” refers to people filming, not performing the actions.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts narrow, deliberately collected robot demonstrations with diverse incidental human data, but does not state that assigned tasks in a data-collection setting suppress everyday physically intelligent interactions.

astra-6.text:
Because if we want robots to help us in everyday life, they need to learn about the variety of things people actually do. Data collected specifically for a robot task is valuable, but you have to decide ahead of time what task to collect, set up the environment, and repeat it. That’s difficult to scale to all the situations a robot might encounter in someone’s home.

People are already doing those activities every day—cooking, cleaning, putting things away. Data captured along the way can show much more variation, including how people recover when something goes wrong.

The challenge is that watching a human do something doesn’t directly tell a robot how to move its own body. So I see this as complementary to robot data: human activity can provide broad knowledge about tasks and the world, while robot experience helps ground that knowledge in actions the robot can actually execute.

r002.rationale: It says task-specific collection requires advance choices, setup, and repetition, but does not state that assigned tasks suppress incidental physically intelligent interactions.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if we want robots to help us in everyday life, we need them to learn from the variety of things people actually do. Data collected specifically for a robot task is useful, but it takes a lot of effort, and it tends to cover a narrow set of tasks and environments. You can’t stage every situation a robot might encounter.

People are already doing these activities every day—cooking, cleaning, organizing things. If we can learn from data captured along the way, there’s an opportunity to get much broader coverage without asking people to repeatedly demonstrate something just for a robot.

The challenge is that watching a person isn’t the same as knowing what actions a robot should take. Our bodies are different, and the data may not capture everything that matters. So I see everyday human data as a rich source of information about tasks and behavior, complemented by robot data that helps ground that knowledge in what the robot can actually do.
